Champion Collapse.description: Deal champion disengages or loses organizational authority mid-cycle. Thread collapses to a single contact with declining responsiveness.

recovery_differentiators.interpretation: Executive sponsor was engaged in 94% of recovered deals vs 39% of lost
Recovered deals had 1.2 more economic buyer meetings

timing_insights.note: Recovered deals tended to intervene earlier in the current stage, suggesting the intervention window closes quickly once a stall signature appears.

interventions.action: Immediate multi-thread: identify 2+ additional stakeholders and make warm intro within 48 hours
interventions.rationale: Champion instability is rarely recoverable through the champion alone — you need to rebuild the thread before access closes entirely

interventions.action: Request executive sponsor introduction through any available channel (board contact, partner, mutual connection)
interventions.rationale: Recovered deals in this pattern overwhelmingly had exec engagement — it compensates for champion loss by creating a second entry point

interventions.action: Map the org chart and identify who inherited the champion's responsibilities or who has budget authority in their absence
interventions.rationale: The deal may not be dead — it may have just relocated inside the org

Competitor Displacement.description: A competitor gains foothold in the deal — often surfacing as pricing pressure, increased objections, and stage regression.

recovery_differentiators.interpretation: Recovered deals had 7.6% lower average discount
Competitive mentions were 1.0 fewer in recovered deals
Recovered deals spent 5 fewer days stuck in stage

timing_insights.note: Recovered deals tended to intervene earlier in the current stage, suggesting the intervention window closes quickly once a stall signature appears.

interventions.action: Accelerate technical validation immediately — schedule a working session, not a demo
interventions.rationale: Competitor displacement deals that recovered almost always completed technical validation before pricing pressure peaked

interventions.action: Get explicit on competitive differentiation: name the competitor, name the gap, and have the champion deliver it internally
interventions.rationale: Deals lost to competitors frequently had ambiguous positioning — recovered deals had a clear, repeatable internal champion message

interventions.action: Resist the discount reflex — offer a pilot or POC extension instead
interventions.rationale: Discounting under competitive pressure in this pattern correlated with loss, not recovery. Deepening product commitment outperformed price concession.

Ghost Stall.description: Prospect goes silent without a stated reason. No activity, no replies, no forward motion. Deal lives in the pipeline but is effectively dead.

recovery_differentiators.interpretation: Recovered reps last touched the deal 6 days sooner
Recovered deals had 0.9 more meetings in the last 30 days

timing_insights.note: Recovered deals tended to intervene earlier in the current stage, suggesting the intervention window closes quickly once a stall signature appears.

interventions.action: Break the email thread — call, text, or LinkedIn. Change the medium before you change the message.
interventions.rationale: Ghost stalls that recovered involved a channel switch early. Additional emails to a prospect who isn't opening emails have near-zero marginal value.

interventions.action: Re-anchor to the original business problem — not the product. 'What changed with [pain point]?' re-opens the conversation without sounding like a follow-up.
interventions.rationale: Ghost stalls are often disengagement from the solution frame, not the problem. Recovered deals re-established problem urgency first.

interventions.action: Set a 10-day deadline internally: if no response after one more creative touch, mark the deal as lost and re-engage in 60 days
interventions.rationale: Deals lingering in Ghost Stall past 30 days without a defined close date have very low recovery rates. Knowing when to re-pipeline is itself a win.

Exec Vacuum.description: Deal is confined to IC-level champion with no economic buyer visibility. Budget decisions happen above the champion's authority level.

recovery_differentiators.interpretation: Executive sponsor was engaged in 89% of recovered deals vs 23% of lost

timing_insights.note: Recovered deals tended to intervene earlier in the current stage, suggesting the intervention window closes quickly once a stall signature appears.

interventions.action: Ask the champion directly: 'Who else needs to say yes for this to move forward?' — then get a warm intro to that person in the same week
interventions.rationale: Recovered Exec Vacuum deals almost always involved the champion helping broker the exec connection, not the rep cold-outreaching above them

interventions.action: Build an internal business case document the champion can take upward — ROI, peer comparisons, and a recommended decision timeline
interventions.rationale: IC-level champions need tools to sell internally. Recovered deals provided this artifact; lost deals assumed the champion would figure it out

interventions.action: If the champion cannot or will not broker exec access after two attempts, escalate to your own leadership for a peer-to-peer outreach
interventions.rationale: VP-to-VP or C-to-C outreach broke Exec Vacuum stalls in recovered deals where champion-led introductions failed

insights.title: Discounting under competitive pressure is anti-correlated with winning
insights.finding: In Competitor Displacement deals, lost deals had an average discount of 22.8% vs 4.2% in won deals. Higher discounts did not improve win rates — they may signal that reps are conceding price when they should be competing on value.
insights.implication: Consider tightening discount approval in competitive deals and investing the saved margin in accelerated technical validation instead.

insights.title: Exec Vacuum hits Enterprise hardest among lost deals
insights.finding: 48% of lost Enterprise deals show Exec Vacuum behavioral signals, compared with SMB (40%) and Mid-Market (44%). Enterprise Exec Vacuum deals look legitimate on paper (VP-level champion, multi-stakeholder) but the true economic buyer sits one or two levels above — reps overestimate champion authority.
insights.implication: Enterprise deal reviews should require named economic-buyer engagement before Proposal Sent, not at Negotiation.

insights.title: Enterprise has the highest rate of misattributed loss reasons
insights.finding: 28.2% of Enterprise lost deals have a stated loss reason that contradicts the behavioral evidence. This is higher than other segments, suggesting Enterprise reps are more likely to default to 'price' or 'timing' without accurately diagnosing why the deal actually failed.
insights.implication: Loss reason analysis for this segment is systematically unreliable. CRM-based competitive intelligence from this segment may be misleading.
